summary: Louisa of Recycle This reconsiders whether teabags can be composted after listing her daily consumables and questioning teabag compostability in a prior post. She recalls Alice in Blogland's finding that teabags contain a synthetic heat seal, then contacts ten tea companies. The note so far reports replies from Tetley and Taylors/Yorkshire, which say the bags are mainly cellulose with small amounts of polypropylene, compostable under proper conditions, though the packs themselves are not.
one_line: Recycle This blogger checks with tea companies on whether teabags, which contain a polypropylene heat seal, can be composted.
key_facts: Louisa wrote the post on 2 June 2011 for the Recycle This website.
Louisa listed all the consumables she used in one day on The Really Good Life and categorised her teabags as "probably not compostable".
Alice in Blogland looked into teabag compostability a few years before 2011 and found that teabags often include synthetic material in the heat sealed bit.
Alice in Blogland's teabag research was about four years old when Louisa wrote her post.
The heat sealed bit of a teabag is typically food grade polypropylene.
Louisa contacted ten tea companies to ask whether their teabags could be composted.
Tetley said the tea bag material is a mixture of mainly cellulose fibres and a small amount of polypropylene fibres to give the heat seal.
Tetley said cellulose fibres and the tea break down under normal composting conditions, leaving very small polypropylene fibres that are normally not seen.
Tetley said teabags need a reasonable amount of time and should be placed in a 'proper', established compost heap.
Tetley said the packs themselves are not compostable and that it is working with its packaging suppliers.
Taylors, which makes Yorkshire tea and the Taylors of Harrogate brand, said its teabag paper has several layers, with one side incorporating a very thin web of meltable polypropylene.
Taylors said legislation classes an item as compostable if it is 95% degradable, and the polypropylene in teabag paper is much less than this.
Taylors said polypropylene is inert and does not react with or damage plants or animals.
Taylors' gardening colleagues reported that teabags compost in around a year or so in a good, healthy compost heap.
Taylors suggested using teabags in a pot on top of crocks and underneath the soil to aid drainage.
